### The Everyday Ingredient Destroying the Planet

**Bloomberg Originals**, *04 05, 2023*

#### Video (11:56)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/8Nj_kIiyrwQ title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

#### Description

Kal Penn investigates the damage being done by the palm oil industry in Indonesia. The product is used in everything from cookies to shampoo, but its production has laid waste to forests all over the globe. With only 20% of palm oil deemed sustainable, Penn looks for solutions, including a UK startup with a lab-made version. But can fake palm oil compete with nature in quality and price?


Getting Warmer is Bloomberg's exclusive new show about climate, clean energy and business, anchored by actor and former White House aide Kal Penn.

Accompany him on his journey as he takes an up-close look at bold climate solutions and discovers new facets of the global transition to clean energy.

In a hosted studio segment, Penn sifts through the overwhelming news about our climate and breaks down the facts and trends to understand with a dose of humor and optimism. Why are the recycling symbols on your plastic cups misleading? How does the carbon credit market work and does it actually help? And what is the future of water in a drought-ridden world?

On the road, Penn meets the innovators, researchers, communities and businesses pivoting to new energy sources and spearheading low-carbon technologies. In documentary segments, Penn speaks to the self-declared “crypto cowboys” of Texas who claim Bitcoin mining can help stabilize the state’s troubled electrical grid, and travels to Nevada to visit the company attempting to build America’s first closed-loop supply chain for electric vehicles. In New York, Penn explores the urban designs proposed to save the city from the next Superstorm Sandy and goes inside New York’s Empire State building to investigate the challenges of decarbonizing our cities and landmarks. 

The show builds on, and includes contributions from, Bloomberg Green’s award-winning team of climate journalists as well as London-based climate storytellers Jack Harries and Alice Aedy. With a focus on the most pressing questions for young viewers, Jack and Alice unpack one big idea each episode. From recycled wastewater to regenerative agriculture and the challenges of a just transition for workers in the energy sector, they’ll break down how countries across the world are finding intriguing solutions to our climate crisis, and outline the challenges ahead.

#### Transcript

##### The ubiquitous palm oil

**0:03** · Palm oil.

**0:04** · You've probably heard of it, yet don't know exactly what it is.

**0:08** · But unless you're on an exclusive nut and berry diet you're probably eating some today.

**0:13** · Or at least rubbed some on your body this morning.

**0:18** · The miraculous, versatile substance is used in thousands of everyday products, from chips and ice cream to shampoo and fuel.

**0:27** · On average, we consume about eight kilograms, or around 18 pounds of palm oil every year.

**0:35** · It comes from the red fruits of an oil palm tree.

**0:43** · Palm is usually not a whole ingredient in something, with the exception of cooking oil.

**0:50** · We're often using a fraction.

**0:52** · It's a part of the fruit, a part of the oil, so it's really easy for that to be invisible within a product.

**1:01** · Seems like the ultimate natural resource, right?

**1:03** · Just pick the fruit off the tree and make stuff with it.

**1:06** · But palm oil has become very controversial in recent years for its cost on the environment.

##### Environmental controversy

**1:12** · Vast swaths of forests have been burned by farmers to make way for oil palm plantations, causing the wholesale destruction of natural habitats, and ultimately contributing to climate change.

**1:24** · There have also been reports of serious labor rights abuses in the industry.

**1:57** · Despite public and private sector efforts to mitigate palm oil's environmental impact, only 20% of the world's palm oil is certified as sustainable today.

##### Seeking sustainable solutions

**2:07** · Like most problems related to the climate crisis there doesn't seem to be one clear solution.

**2:13** · The damage being done by the palm oil industry is significant and not going away anytime soon.

**2:19** · But farmers, big companies, and scientists are working in their own ways to try to chip away at its negative effects.

**2:27** · The way that we produce food now is a modern miracle, but it's also having an enormous impact on the environment.

**2:33** · We have to create changes.

**2:34** · We have to work towards creating these novel foodstuffs, which have much lower impact, which are healthy, and delicious, and different to what we had before.

##### Smallholder farmer challenges

**3:26** · Edy is one of 16 million people working in the palm oil industry in Indonesia, the world's biggest palm oil producer, churning out about 47 million tons in 2020 alone.

**4:00** · About 40% of the oil palm plantations in Indonesia are owned by small scale farmers like Edy, who have less than 25 hectares of land.

**4:10** · But many small holders didn't have an understanding of sustainable farming.

**4:14** · Slashing and burning the forest was common because it was the cheapest and fastest way to make land to grow oil palm trees.

**4:22** · Between 2005 and 2013, almost half of the deforestation in Indonesia was linked to oil palm cultivation.

**4:30** · 2015 was the worst year.

**4:32** · Between June and October, fires burned an area roughly the size of Rwanda, or the US state of Maryland.

**4:40** · Researchers linked the toxic haze, which lingered for weeks, to more than 100,000 premature deaths in Indonesia, and in neighboring countries like Malaysia and Singapore.

**5:07** · In 2016, Indonesian president Joko Widodo imposed a moratorium on new permits for clearing forest and peatland for oil palm cultivation.

**5:18** · Deforestation linked to palm oil is still happening, but educational campaigns and stricter law enforcement have reduced it significantly.

**5:28** · More farmers like Edy have joined small holders associations like this one.

**5:32** · With financial support from NGOs and big companies, they've got certification from institutes like the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, or RSPO.

**5:42** · Sustainable palm oil has to meet strict standards, such as using best farming practices, conserving the environment, and considering employees benefits and rights.

**5:52** · But Edy's only one of a tiny number of certified small holders because many farmers don't have the resources or access to get certified.

**6:00** · And challenges still remain after being certified.

##### Big oil industry impact

**6:28** · The other piece of the puzzle is big palm oil companies.

**6:35** · Here at Golden Agri-Resources, we have more than 500,000 hectares of palm oil plantations across Indonesia, but we also buy fresh fruit bunches from other producers of palm.

**6:48** · And so we actually trade and process closer to around six to eight million tons of what's called crude palm oil, or palm related products.

**7:00** · Harvested fruit bunches are sent to mills and then refineries for processing.

**7:06** · The outer orange part of the fruit creates crude palm oil, which can be turned into many different products, like cooking oil and biofuel.

**7:14** · The white creamy substance inside the kernel creates palm kernel oil, which is used in cosmetics, soaps, and hand sanitizers.

**7:24** · In the past, criticism of the industry in terms of its impact on forests, wildlife, and even on local communities, sadly, was justified.

**7:41** · We wanna be able to produce the equivalent of a million hectares of land on that half a million hectares of land.

**7:48** · So focusing on using biotechnology techniques, but also really good farming practices.

**7:56** · But full traceability of the supply chain still remains a challenge.

**8:00** · Third party plantations are usually in remote locations spanning millions of hectares.

**8:06** · Another challenge is consumer commitment.

**8:08** · About 20% of the world's palm oil was certified as sustainable, but buyers only bought half of it.

**8:15** · So the greatest demand still comes from buyers in Europe and the US, to a certain extent Australia.

**8:22** · However, the largest volumes are sold in countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, India, and China, where demand for a sustainable product is still very low.

##### Developing lab alternatives

**8:40** · Making palm oil production sustainable is crucial, but some scientists are hoping we could stop using it completely.

**8:46** · But the researchers working on an alternative to palm oil will need to ensure their products are competitive in quality and price.

**8:54** · Ultimately, there's no mystery to palm oil.

**8:56** · It's a relatively simple group of compounds of which other organisms can make as well.

**9:01** · And that's what we've been able to mimic with the yeast.

**9:04** · So this process is very similar to brewing beer, technology we've known about for thousands of years.

**9:10** · Where, when you brew beer, you take sugars and grow a brewing yeast on them, which produces ethanol, which we can drink.

**9:18** · In our process, we're using natural yeast, which naturally make edible oils.

**9:24** · Finding the right yeast is key.

**9:26** · After a few years of researching and experimenting, the team found metschnikowia pulcherrima, a yeast that grows on the surface of grapes all over the world.

**9:35** · And then they spent another eight years developing the yeast and the process to grow it.

**9:40** · Here, we have to use large drums of eight kilograms of the sugar.

**9:44** · It's dragged into the reactor here and then fed to the yeast.

**9:47** · Now here we have 50 liters of culture, and this is enough to make kilograms of yeast in a week.

**9:54** · This is also a really good mimic to demonstrate what an industrial process will truly look like on the large scale.

**10:02** · So the yeast we selected at first didn't make much oil, but it had a number of other attributes which allow us to produce it on the large scale.

**10:10** · So it could be produced under a wide temperature range.

**10:14** · It could be produced under a wide range of pHs.

**10:17** · It also can use a whole range of sugars, saccharides, and proteins to grow, which allows us to use waste resources very efficiently.

**10:25** · The team has completed research and development, successfully fed the yeast with waste food like coffee grounds, and agricultural leftovers like wheat straw and sawdust.

**10:35** · Now, they're running a pilot, producing kilograms of palm oil substitute per week.

**10:40** · And aim to increase that to tons per week within a year.

**10:44** · So here we have the yeast.

**10:45** · And you have these giant cells, which are then full of oil, which we can extract.

**10:51** · A startup has been spun out from the project, raising over $2.5 million, with the goal to bring the product to grocery store shelves.

**10:59** · In the last few decades, we've seen people really starting to choose alternative products, alternative analogs to meat, for example.

**11:06** · Products like yeast protein from corn.

**11:09** · We see ourselves as continuing that journey and being the next generation of novel foods.

##### Future of the industry

**11:15** · Regardless of what the future holds, the palm oil industry needs to make serious changes today.

##### Transcript

###### The history of extinction

**0:02** · [MUSIC] The California Golden Bear The Great Auk The Passenger pigeon The Tasmanian tiger The Pinta Island tortoise The Golden toad All dead. And the killer is right there in the room with you.

**0:22** · [MUSIC] The walls of France’s Lascaux cave hold some of humankind’s earliest art, almost mythical species: a wooly rhinoceros, enormous-antlered Megaloceros elk and massive aurochs. The artists lived on, became us, but those cave walls are the last place that those animals still run. They’re gone. Extinct.

**0:51** · We all pretty much understand extinction, it’s when a species kicks the proverbial bucket, it rides off into the great biological sunset, bites the dust from whence it came and shall return, which is all just a pretty way of saying that every last one of them dies.

**1:05** · Even kids are used to the idea that sometimes groups of living things just… don’t exist anymore. Okay, mostly don’t exist.

###### Discovering mass events

**1:13** · But extinction, as a thing, is a surprisingly new concept. In the 1790’s, by studying various fossils, naturalist Georges Cuvier was the first to show that they were not from living, yet undiscovered creatures, as many thought, but from what he called “lost species”.

**1:29** · In the decades to come, scientists like Charles Lyell and ol' Chuck Darwin began to popularize the idea that Earth’s processes, like geology, evolution, and even extinction, did occur, just very, very, verrrry slowly. So slowly that we’d surely never actually see something go extinct. The idea of so-called catastrophic change was just impossible… It wasn’t until the 1980’s that scientists were able to shake that idea. Geologist Walter Alvarez was puzzled by the sudden disappearance of tiny aquatic fossils between two rock layers that dated from about 66 million years ago, the same age as the last dinosaurs.

**2:01** · With the help of his Nobel Prize winning father, he analyzed the chemistry of that boundary and found iridium levels that were off the charts. Now, there’s usually not much iridium in Earth’s crust, but it’s very common in asteroids. So Alvarez’s theory? A 10-km wide rock collided with Earth, wiping out 75% of Earth’s plants and animals. To be honest scientists kinda laughed at it… until the 1991 discovery of the Chicxulub crater near the Yucatan peninsula finally settled it.

**2:36** · Everything alive today is a descendent of a survivor of that terrible, horrible, no good, very bad day, the so-called Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction event, the most recent of the Big 5.

###### The big five extinctions

**2:50** · You should feel pretty lucky. When we look at all of Earth’s fossil record together, 98% of the species that have ever lived are extinct,. Only they haven’t always disappeared at a constant rate.

**3:02** · In the history of life on Earth, we know of 5 different mass extinctions, when a majority of life on Earth at the time disappeared in the blink of a geologic eye.

**3:13** · Besides the most recent dino-killer, there’s the Triassic-Jurassic, Late Devonian, Ordivician-Silurian, and the worst of all, the End Permian. This was the mother of mass extinctions, it wiped out as many as 96% of Earth’s species, so it got the best nickname: The Great Dying.

**3:34** · We’ve learned about all these just in time to get some bad news: We are in the 6th mass extinction, and this time, we are the asteroid.

###### The sixth mass extinction

**3:46** · The hard facts of life mean that even when things are going pretty well on Earth, there’s a background rate of extinction. Among mammals, for instance, we’d expect to see one species go extinct every 700 years, or maybe one amphibian every thousand years.

**4:00** · Studies of current extinction rates say we’re roughly one thousand times past that, and in some groups, like amphibians, are disappearing forty-five thousand times faster than normal.

**4:13** · And since there are so many species still unknown or uncharacterized, all of those numbers are probably underestimates.

**4:19** · Goodbye, gastric brooding frog, Pyrenean ibex, the Fomosan clouded leopard. We could have been friends.

**4:29** · So how do we know we’re to blame?

**4:32** · Around 13,000 years ago, as Earth thawed from its most recent big freeze, all of our favorite weird megafauna like the wooly mammoth, Smilodon, and our old friend Megatherium disappeared from the Earth, thanks to a changing climate and the invention of sharp stabby hunting tools. I really wish we had saved the 8-foot long beaver though. That would be awesome.

**4:53** · Along the way, through hunting and farming, humans have been altering ecosystems in small but significant ways, but since the Industrial Revolution, man we have really kicked it into overdrive.

**5:05** · With the exception of maybe the first bacteria to breathe oxygen into the air, no living thing has ever altered life on Earth to the degree that we have, which is why scientists now refer to current epoch as the Anthropocene.

###### Drivers of species loss

**5:18** · "We are the ultimate problem. There are 7 billion people on the planet, we tend to destroy critical habitats where species live, we tend to be warming the planet, we tend to be very careless about moving species around the planet."

**5:32** · According to a 2014 paper by Stuart Pimm in Science (link in the doobly do), the main cause of the current extinction is human population growth and increased consumption. But those two things lead to a whole mess of threats: The most obvious are climate change and habitat destruction. Scientists found that most land species have very small ranges, so they can’t just pack up and move when we cut down their forest or turn it into a desert.

**5:55** · Ocean species have more freedom to move to better waters, unless they’re coral reefs, but thanks to the highest atmospheric CO2 concentrations in 800,000+ years turning the oceans more acidic, anything with a calcium based shell has nowhere to run… or swim. If current trends hold up and the ocean hits pH 7.8 by end of century, it could wipe out ⅓ of the species in the ocean.

**6:23** · Then there’s the invaders! Thanks to a species of snake hitching a ride on military cargo in the 1940s, Guam has lost all of its native birds. "I have had it with these (invasive) snakes on this (Guam-bound cargo) plane" In Africa’s Lake Victoria, 100s of species of cichlid fish species vanished after fishermen introduced the Nile Perch. Go us! We’re erasing species faster than we can even name them.

**6:50** · Stanford’s Rodolfo Dirzo says that in the past 40 years, invertebrate populations, which might make up 97% of species on Earth, have declined 45% worldwide, and that’s just the ones we know about. (Link in the doobly do to that one too) You have to feel worst for the amphibians. Over the past 350 million years, they’ve survived multiple mass extinctions, but this time we’re giving them all we’ve got.

**7:17** · Dirzo gives this loss of animal life a rather harmless sounding name: Defaunation. But there is nothing cute about it. There is not a group of living things on Earth today that is not threatened by the current and coming extinction. That includes us.

###### Why saving species matters

**7:34** · Extinction is about more than gorillas, tigers, polar bears, and rhinos, and the dozens of other “famous” or “charismatic” species out there. Those are all important and worth saving, but we need to care just as much about the humble beetles, the ugly little worms, and the slimy frogs.

**7:52** · Every species, big or small, panda or protozoa, is important and worth saving, whether or not we understand exactly why it’s worth saving.

**8:02** · John Muir once said, “When we try to pick out anything by itself we find that it is bound fast by a thousand invisible cords that cannot be broken, to everything in the universe.”

**8:15** · I’ve put some links down in the description where you can get to know some of Earth’s less-loved endangered species. Go make friends with one.

**8:23** · Our knowledge and understanding of the planet’s ecosystems may be incomplete, but our effect on them knows no bounds. I hope the same tools and technology that we’ve used to push life on Earth to the edge might also give us power to bring ‘em back.

**8:39** · So what are we gonna do? Let’s talk about it down there.

**8:43** · Stay curious.

**8:44** · If you want to read more about the brilliant and tragic stories of extinction in this age of humans, check out "The Sixth Extinction" by Elizabeth Kolbert, link in the description.

#### Climate change can money stop deforestation

##### Video (9:44)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/EXkbdELr4EQ title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Tree-planting has been hailed as a solution to climate change. But how much can trees really do to tackle global warming? See our research here: https://econ.st/32HXvXY

Click here to subscribe to The Economist on YouTube: https://econ.st/2xvTKdy 

Summer 2019 - More than 38,000 fires raged across the Amazon. Fires that were man-made. Over the past 50 years almost 17% of the world’s largest rainforest has been cleared. And globally deforestation has almost doubled in just five years.

Since the start of human civilisation it’s estimated that the number of trees around the world has fallen by almost half. Clearing forests increases carbon-dioxide levels but planting them could store away some of the carbon already in the atmosphere.

This woman runs safaris in England. Guests are not only here to see wild animals - they’re here to see wild trees.

Almost 20 years ago Isabella Tree—yes that is her real name-handed 1,400 hectares of Sussex farmland back to nature, by doing, well nothing. She thinks this is the best way to use the land to help tackle climate change.

To stabilise the climate global carbon emissions need to drop to net zero by 2050. Simon Lewis is a professor of global change science.

And there’s never been more global ambition to plant trees. In 2014, 51 countries pledged to plant over 3.5m square kilometres of forest by 2030 - an area slightly larger than India. The 2030 target looks likely to be met. But there’s a catch… 

Monoculture tree plantations like eucalyptus grow quickly but the trees are harvested every ten or so years releasing much of the carbon stored in the tree back into the atmosphere - which means that, according to some studies they’ll store only around one-fortieth of the carbon natural forests do over the long term.

In fact, those pledges to plant millions of trees actually promise to store 26bn tonnes less carbon than they could. Sometimes the motives for planting forests are less green than they might appear. By 2020 Ireland ought to have cut greenhouse-gas emissions by 20% below 2005 levels. But at current rates it will have reduced them by only 5%. Planting forests might help Ireland avoid massive penalties for missing EU targets because the potential carbon these forests could store in the future can be counted as a carbon credit today. In the 1920s Ireland had the lowest forest cover in Europe at around 1%. That’s now risen to 11% and the government has set a target to cover 18% of the land with forest by 2046.

And now local community groups are protesting against these monoculture tree plantations. They say they’re doing more harm than good.

Tree-planting programmes invariably have an impact on the people living nearby. In east Africa one project is demonstrating what can be achieved

when there’s genuine buy-in from the local communities. Green Ethiopia is a mixed-tree planting charity.

The land is communally owned and co-operatives of local women receive benefits for planting trees which are protected from being harvested. Here conserving is just as important as planting. Green Ethiopia assesses whether the condition of the land is good enough to regenerate by itself. When it is—on about a third of the area the charity runs they leave it alone. Just like Isabella Tree, back in England.

Monoculture plantations are often preferred because they make money. So some experts are looking to a future where carbon payments could create financial incentives for natural forests. Ultimately though, the trouble with trees tackling climate change is space

🔎 ABOUT THIS PROJECT

===============================

Over recent decades, large swathes of Slovakia’s wetlands have been lost. They have been drained to make way for agriculture as a result of the construction of dams for hydroelectric power, as well as for timber production. Wetlands are an integral part of the Danube floodplain landscape in Slovakia and draining them to plant trees has detrimental impacts on the environment. Wetlands store large amounts of carbon and are home to a diversity of plant and animal species that are specially adapted to the wet conditions. One of these species is the nationally endangered and endemic Pannonian root vole, which has declined drastically in Slovakia in response to disappearing wetlands. This project will turn forest back into a wetland by digging 650 meters of ditches. This will kickstart a “flood” of change and bring back a healthy functioning, sustainable and wilder ecosystem.

Read more about this project here: https://www.mossy.earth/projects/restoring-wetlands

##### Description

Watch the full first episode of Human Footprint here: https://youtu.be/m36E3n7y3mY

Ever heard of the phrase "when pet pythons outgrow their owners"? Well, host Shane Campbell-Staton is about to take us on an adventure to find out what happens next in this episode of Human Footprint. Join Shane as he meets bounty hunter Donna Kalil, exotic animal trader Hillary Dupont, and biologists Matthew McCollister and Kristen Hart as they battle the invasive Burmese Pythons of the Everglades.

Human Footprint is a show that delves into the impact of humans on the planet. Join Shane as he travels from farms to restaurants, from high-tech labs to street markets, and from forests to cities to uncover the consequences of our unique history. Are you ready to explore our past, present, and future as a species?

#### How one scientist took on the chemical industry

**TED-Ed**, *03 17, 2020*

##### Video (5:22)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/ezVEzCmiXM4 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Discover the groundbreaking environmental work of Rachel Carson, whose book “Silent Spring” explores how human actions threaten the balance of nature. 

--

In 1958, after receiving a letter describing the deaths of songbirds due to the pesticide known as DDT, Rachel Carson began an investigation into the misuse of chemicals and their toll on nature. In 1962, she published her findings in “Silent Spring,” which immediately drew both applause and impassioned dissent. How did this biologist and writer ignite such controversy? Mark Lytle investigates.

Lesson by Mark Lytle, directed by Héloïse Dorsan Rachet.

##### Transcript

###### Intro

**0:06** · In 1958, Rachel Carson received a letter describing songbirds suddenly dropping from tree branches.

**0:13** · The writer blamed their deaths on a pesticide called DDT that exterminators had sprayed on a nearby marsh.

**0:19** · The letter was the push Carson needed to investigate DDT.

**0:23** · She had already heard from scientists and conservationists who were worried that rampant use of the pesticide posed a threat to fish, birds, and possibly humans.

**0:33** · She began to make inquiries through government contacts from her years working in the United States Bureau of Fisheries.

**0:40** · She asked: “what has already silenced the voices of spring?”

###### Silent Spring

**0:45** · In 1962, Carson published her findings in "Silent Spring."

**0:50** · Her book documented the misuse of chemicals and their toll on nature and human health.

**0:56** · "Silent Spring" immediately drew both applause and impassioned dissent— along with vicious personal attacks on the author.

**1:04** · How did this mild-mannered biologist and writer ignite such controversy?

**1:10** · Carson began her career as a hardworking graduate student, balancing her studies in biology at John Hopkins University with part time jobs.

**1:18** · Still, she had to leave school before completing her doctorate to provide for her ailing father and sister.

**1:25** · Carson found part time work with the Bureau of Fisheries writing for a radio program on marine biology.

**1:31** · Her ability to write materials that could hold the general public’s attention impressed her superiors, and in 1936, she became the second woman to be hired at the Bureau full time.

**1:43** · In 1941, she published the first of three books on the ocean, combining science with lyrical meditations on underwater worlds.

**1:52** · These explorations resonated with a wide audience.

**1:56** · In "Silent Spring," Carson turned her attention to the ways human actions threaten the balance of nature.

**2:03** · DDT was originally used during World War II to shield crops from insects and protect soldiers from insect-borne diseases.

**2:12** · After the war, it was routinely sprayed in wide swaths to fight pests, often with unforeseen results.

**2:19** · One attempt to eradicate fire ants in the southern U.S.

**2:22** · killed wildlife indiscriminately, but did little to eliminate the ants.

###### DDT

**2:29** · In spite of this and other mishaps, the US Department of Agriculture and chemical companies extolled the benefits of DDT.

**2:37** · There was little regulation or public awareness about its potential harm.

**2:41** · But Carson showed how the overuse of chemicals led to the evolution of resistant species— which, in turn, encouraged the development of deadlier chemicals.

**2:51** · Since DDT does not dissolve in water, she asserted that over time it would accumulate in the environment, the bodies of insects, the tissues of animals who consume those insects, and eventually humans.

**3:04** · She suggested that exposure to DDT might alter the structure of genes, with unknown consequences for future generations.

**3:13** · The response to "Silent Spring" was explosive.

**3:17** · For many people the book was a call to regulate substances capable of catastrophic harm.

**3:22** · Others objected that Carson hadn’t mentioned DDT’s role controlling the threat insects posed to human health.

**3:30** · Former Secretary of Agriculture Ezra Taft Benson demanded to know “why a spinster with no children was so concerned about genetics?”

**3:40** · and dismissed Carson as “probably a Communist.”

**3:44** · A lawyer for a pesticide manufacturer alluded to Carson and her supporters as “sinister influences” aiming to paint businesses as “immoral.”

**3:55** · In reality, Carson had focused on the dangers of chemicals because they weren’t widely understood, while the merits were well publicized.

**4:03** · She rejected the prevailing belief that humans should and could control nature.

**4:08** · Instead, she challenged people to cultivate “maturity and mastery, not of nature, but of ourselves.”

###### Environmentalists

**4:16** · Carson died of cancer in 1964, only two years after the publication of "Silent Spring."

**4:23** · Her work galvanized a generation of environmental activists.

**4:28** · In 1969, under pressure from environmentalists, Congress passed the National Environmental Policy Act that required federal agencies to evaluate environmental impacts of their actions.

**4:41** · To enforce the act, President Richard Nixon created the Environmental Protection Agency.

**4:47** · And in 1972, the EPA issued a partial ban on the use of DDT.

**4:53** · Long after her death, Rachel Carson continued to advocate for nature through the lingering impact of her writing.

#### Is “Environmental DNA” the Future of Conservation  Wild Hope Explains

**Nature on PBS**, *04 13, 2026*

##### Video (5:28)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/WG_ryk_0zM8 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

What if you could discover every animal in an ecosystem…without ever seeing them? Environmental DNA (or eDNA) does exactly that. By collecting tiny samples of soil, water, or even air, researchers can identify dozens (or even hundreds) of species from the genetic traces they leave behind. 

From tracking predators in Detroit to uncovering rare species in Ecuador’s rainforests, eDNA is helping conservationists make better decisions to protect biodiversity. Learn how it works, why it matters, and how this cutting-edge science is reshaping the future of conservation.


Follow us: https://www.instagram.com/wildhopetv/ 

Join our community: https://wildhope.tv

Get our newsletter: http://eepurl.com/irGMng 

Share this with a friend!

##### Transcript

###### The challenge of biodiversity

**0:00** · SPEAKER 1: To protect wildlife, conservationists need to first answer what might seem like a simple question.

**0:06** · Which species actually live in the habitats they're trying to save?

**0:11** · This question might be difficult to answer, especially in dense and complex habitats like rainforests or shifting landscapes around cities.

**0:23** · Ecologists have a long list of methods at their disposal-- radio collars, camera traps, acoustic monitoring, and even good, old-fashioned direct observation.

**0:34** · SPEAKER 2: See where it went down?

**0:35** · SPEAKER 1: But the newest tool has the potential to be the most comprehensive yet.

###### Introducing eDNA

**0:40** · By collecting small samples of soil, water, or air, scientists can now create a genetic roster of every species that calls an environment home.

**0:51** · It's a tool known as environmental DNA.

**1:02** · Here in Detroit, environmental DNA, or eDNA, is revolutionizing our ability to survey wildlife.

###### Urban wildlife tracking

**1:10** · Dr. Nyeema Harris and Dr. Jane Hallam are tracking how predators, like coyotes, travel through the urban landscape and how their range overlaps with the other wildlife, with local pets, and with humans.

**1:23** · Camera traps have been the go-to method for this type of research for decades, but now with eDNA, scientists can detect species without ever catching them on camera.

**1:34** · Animal shed DNA constantly through scat or hair or skin cells.

**1:40** · Samples from a single habitat might contain this so-called trace DNA from dozens or hundreds of wild species.

**1:50** · NYEEMA C. HARRIS: We get that species list from the cameras because we see the images.

**1:54** · When we're collecting the eDNA, we also then get a species list.

**1:58** · So that means when we've collected the soil and we've done the molecular analysis, the DNA that we've detected has come from 24 different mammal species in the city of Detroit, and some of those species we don't actually see on the camera.

**2:15** · SPEAKER 1: EDNA isn't new.

###### Advances in DNA analysis

**2:17** · It's been used to detect wildlife since the early 2000s, but the technology continues to advance.

**2:23** · Today, scientists can identify species using much smaller fragments of DNA than ever before.

**2:30** · Trace DNA collected in the field is replicated through a technique called Polymerase Chain Reaction, or PCR.

**2:37** · It makes millions of identical copies of the genetic material, which can then be cross-checked against a DNA database of known species.

**2:46** · Dr. JANE HALLAM: This is a bit like forensics.

**2:47** · Environmental DNA tends to be quite broken up because it's been exposed to the elements, and it's been broken down by ultraviolet light from the sun.

**2:56** · So that DNA isn't in great shape.

**2:57** · It tends to be in quite small fragments, but that's enough for us to detect the species.

**3:04** · SPEAKER 1: The size of those DNA fragments is key to why environmental DNA is such a powerful technique.

###### Barcoding genetic sequences

**3:10** · For context, the genome of an animal like a coyote includes roughly 2.5 billion base pairs.

**3:16** · But you don't need a complete genome to identify a sample source.

**3:20** · Certain small DNA sequences are shared among all members of a species.

**3:26** · They act like the barcodes you see at the store.

**3:29** · And when fragments of eDNA from the wild are cross-checked against a database of existing barcodes, we can match the fragments to the species they came from.

**3:39** · Early eDNA methods required a barcode 100 base pairs or longer in order to identify a species.

**3:46** · But today, with new sequencing technology and better computing power, fragments as small as 30 base pairs are often enough for a successful species match.

**3:59** · This has broadened the use of eDNA to some amazing extremes.

###### The future of conservation

**4:03** · Even ancient, degraded DNA from soil 2 million years old can reveal extinct species, like woolly mammoths.

**4:13** · And in dense environments like the rainforests of Ecuador, where vegetation makes wildlife surveys difficult, eDNA has become an essential tool.

**4:23** · Traditional genetic analysis can sample just one species at a time.

**4:28** · Now, eDNA can sample hundreds at once.

**4:33** · To the teams on the ground, eDNA is a low-cost, low-disturbance tool that detects species that are otherwise extremely difficult to find.

**4:46** · From the rainforests of Ecuador to the streets of Detroit, results from eDNA are directly impacting environmental policy.

**4:54** · Conservationists everywhere are embracing eDNA, the latest powerful tool at their disposal.

**5:01** · Finally a way to reveal an entire ecosystem worth of life in a single scoop of dirt.

#### New Trees Won’t Solve Global Warming

##### Description

The idea of tree-planting to offset carbon emissions has boomed in recent years. It’s cheap, appealing to consumers and companies, and allows us to feel like we’re “taking action.” But many tree planting programs don’t actually increase forest cover, improve biodiversity or sequester carbon. In this segment from Getting Warmer, climate storyteller Jack Harries explores whether planting trees is actually the best solution to the climate crisis.


Getting Warmer is Bloomberg's exclusive new show about climate, clean energy and business, anchored by actor and former White House aide Kal Penn.

Accompany him on his journey as he takes an up-close look at bold climate solutions and discovers new facets of the global transition to clean energy.

In a hosted studio segment, Penn sifts through the overwhelming news about our climate and breaks down the facts and trends to understand with a dose of humor and optimism. Why are the recycling symbols on your plastic cups misleading? How does the carbon credit market work and does it actually help? And what is the future of water in a drought-ridden world?

On the road, Penn meets the innovators, researchers, communities and businesses pivoting to new energy sources and spearheading low-carbon technologies. In documentary segments, Penn speaks to the self-declared “crypto cowboys” of Texas who claim Bitcoin mining can help stabilize the state’s troubled electrical grid, and travels to Nevada to visit the company attempting to build America’s first closed-loop supply chain for electric vehicles. In New York, Penn explores the urban designs proposed to save the city from the next Superstorm Sandy and goes inside New York’s Empire State building to investigate the challenges of decarbonizing our cities and landmarks. 

The show builds on, and includes contributions from, Bloomberg Green’s award-winning team of climate journalists as well as London-based climate storytellers Jack Harries and Alice Aedy. With a focus on the most pressing questions for young viewers, Jack and Alice unpack one big idea each episode. From recycled wastewater to regenerative agriculture and the challenges of a just transition for workers in the energy sector, they’ll break down how countries across the world are finding intriguing solutions to our climate crisis, and outline the challenges ahead.

#### Seed Dispersal and Habitat Fragmentation  HHMI BioInteractive Video

**biointeractive**, *06 07, 2017*

##### Video (8:02)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/0m6AjWZ2p8I title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Watch researchers follow brown spider monkeys in a tropical forest of Colombia to determine which plant seeds they are dispersing. Seed dispersers are critical to the forest’s ability to grow and regenerate. 

As the tropical forests of Colombia are cleared for farmland and cattle ranches, the remaining patches of forest become fewer, smaller and further apart from each other threatening the survival of the animals that live there, including brown spider monkeys. Brown spider monkeys are critical seed dispersers and as their numbers decrease the forest is less able to regenerate. Andres Link and Carolina Urbina Malo of Los Andes University in Colombia are identifying the seeds that spider monkeys disperse to better understand the monkeys’ role in the forest and to predict which plants will be most affected by fragmentation. Once the seeds have been catalogued, Link and colleagues replant them to create corridors between isolated patches of forest.

For more information and related materials, visit HHMI BioInteractive: https://www.biointeractive.org/classroom-resources/seed-dispersal-and-habitat-fragmentation

Why are the recycling symbols on your plastic cups misleading? How does the carbon credit market work and does it actually help? And what is the future of water in a drought-ridden world?

On the road, Penn meets the innovators, researchers, communities and businesses pivoting to new energy sources and spearheading low-carbon technologies. In documentary segments, Penn speaks to the self-declared “crypto cowboys” of Texas who claim Bitcoin mining can help stabilize the state’s troubled electrical grid, and travels to Nevada to visit the company attempting to build America’s first closed-loop supply chain for electric vehicles. In New York, Penn explores the urban designs proposed to save the city from the next Superstorm Sandy and goes inside New York’s Empire State building to investigate the challenges of decarbonizing our cities and landmarks. 

The show builds on, and includes contributions from, Bloomberg Green’s award-winning team of climate journalists as well as London-based climate storytellers Jack Harries and Alice Aedy. With a focus on the most pressing questions for young viewers, Jack and Alice unpack one big idea each episode. From recycled wastewater to regenerative agriculture and the challenges of a just transition for workers in the energy sector, they’ll break down how countries across the world are finding intriguing solutions to our climate crisis, and outline the challenges ahead.

#### The Florida River Becoming a Refuge for Manatees  WILD HOPE

**Nature on PBS**, *01 08, 2024*

##### Video (15:34)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/1sVU9RocV7M title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Crystal River has long been a safe haven for the Florida manatee, but when an invasive algae wiped out the eelgrass that manatees need for food, the community rallied to restore the river and save the animals that call it home.

After an unexpected storm forever changed Crystal River more than three decades ago, Lisa Moore founded Save Crystal River to rally the community to garner funding for a massive restoration project. Sea and Shoreline’s Jessica Mailliez demonstrates the dirty work they do to remove invasive algae and restore native eelgrass. This transformation has allowed Florida manatees to return to Crystal River, but for those living along the west coast of the state, the situation is much more dire.  

There, manatees are declining fast — nearly two thousand have died from starvation since 2020 along the Indian River Lagoon. Zoo Tampa has been rescuing as many starving manatees as they can hold, saving them from death and prepping them for re-release into the wild. Fortunately for the manatees ready to return to the wild, they have a safe destination: Crystal River. The strides made in that small community hold promise for a path forward for manatees across the state.

##### Description

The UK is one of the most nature depleted countries in the world, but the Knepp Estate in southern England is trying to change that. Over the past 20 years they have set about rewilding the estate, turning it from a degraded farm to a thriving wildlife habitat.

##### Description

Indonesia is building a new capital city in the heart of Borneo to replace sinking Jakarta. As construction transforms one of the world's most biodiverse rainforests, scientists and Indigenous communities are racing to record the sounds of the forest—and preserve generations of ecological knowledge before it's lost.

This story was supported by a grant from @PulitzerCenter (https://pulitzercenter.org/)

#### Thornforest Restoring the Wildlands of South Texas

**Cornell Lab of Ornithology**, *01 30, 2026*

##### Video (14:42)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/nOJmiR1U4FU title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

The thornforest of Texas’s Lower Rio Grande Valley is one of the most biodiverse ecosystems in North America, attracting birdwatchers and wildlife enthusiasts from around the globe. It supports over 500 species of migratory and resident birds, 300 species of butterflies, 1,200 species of plants, and approximately 50 species of mammals, including the last remaining population of ocelots in the United States. This rugged, spiny habitat is emblematic of the region and closely linked to the cultures and communities that live there. But despite its importance to people and wildlife, the thornforest that historically covered most of the Lower Rio Grande Valley has been reduced to a mere 5-10% of its original extent, and many of the species that call it home are threatened or endangered. "Thornforest: Restoring the Wildlands of South Texas" weaves stunning wildlife footage with expert voices to share the story of this unique ecosystem and the organizations and communities that are coming together to save it.

##### Description

We’re building floating city wetlands to bring nature back to Bristol.

🌱 Join us to rewild the planet: https://planetwild.com/join/m43

Many cities, like Bristol, were built on wetlands. But to make space for us to live, huge drainage systems were created and the water was removed. This has led to some massive problems: less space for nature, more polluted water, and a greater risk of flooding.

That’s why, in our 43rd mission, we went to Bristol and partnered with WWT to bring wetlands back to the city. For this mission, we're also joined by sustainability creator @itsSamBentley. 

Together, we're building floating wetlands in Bristol Hardor. We're also helping develop a miniature “wetland-in-a-box” that enables anyone with a drainpipe to rewild their city.  

Special thanks to FLYNN for providing a render of the upcoming "wetland-in-a-box".

Sam Bentley is a sustainability content creator and climate activist.

##### Description

We’re turning an abandoned fish farm into a beaver paradise

🌱 Join us to rewild the planet: https://planetwild.com/join/m41

Beavers are nature’s ultimate engineers. By building dams, digging canals and keeping water in the landscape, they can turn dry land into thriving wetlands full of biodiversity.

They were nearly wiped out but against all odds, they’ve made an incredible comeback.

Our partner Rewilding Oder Delta is helping secure that return. That's why we teamed up with them for our 41st mission, and purchased a 20-hectare abandoned fish farm in Poland to turn into a natural beaver paradise.

###### The Great Beaver Comeback


**0:00** · What if there was a surprisingly simple way to more than double biodiversity, boost water quality, and prevent catastrophic floods and droughts?

**0:09** · Right now, a movement is taking shape to bring back long-lost ecosystems in record time using the power of beavers. And we thought, "Well, that looks like fun. Let's try it ourselves." This place we're standing at, it used to be a giant fish farm until very recently. And now it's abandoned and doing absolutely nothing for nature.

**0:29** · But that's going to change big time because the Planet Wild community is buying this entire dried-out piece of land and turning it into a massive beaver playground. A beaver population has already been spotted nearby, and if everything goes to plan, they will transform this barren wasteland into a thriving ecosystem much, much faster than any human construction crew ever could.

**0:55** · Join me on a fascinating journey to learn all about nature's number one ecosystem engineers, the crazy comeback story they've had after near extinction, and how they will turn all of this into this. We are Planet Wild. Welcome to Mission 41. (charming music) Everything you see here around me was created by one creature.

###### How beavers transform ecosystems

**1:20** · (upbeat music) Introducing even a single beaver into a landscape creates an explosion of biodiversity far more than what we see with any other living thing. (upbeat music) And that's simply because they bring water into the landscape, turning dry land into a mosaic of deep ponds, complex canals, and shallow wetlands. These are perfect breeding grounds for fish and amphibians. The wooden dams and the still water attract millions of insects, providing a feast for all kinds of birds.

**1:58** · The abundance of water and diverse vegetation also attracts larger mammals like elk, deer, martens, and even wolves. All of this makes beaver wetlands pretty much impossible to replicate artificially.

**2:11** · What beavers do can help restore our landscape much better than we can do with our engineering.

**2:19** · This is Frauke.

###### Meet our partner

**2:21** · She's worked alongside beavers for the last 17 years, and she's part of our friends at Rewilding Oder Delta who are doing pioneering work to bring back Europe's most iconic wildlife species, including lynx, sea eagles, elk, and even the European bison. But now it's the beavers' time. Three years ago, together with their Polish partner, they purchased a piece of land to turn it into a nature reserve and restore its lost wetland.

**2:48** · The plan: create a protected area and then simply step back and let the local beavers take the reins. And as I got to see firsthand on my exploration with Frauke, the plan actually worked. But now we have our eyes on a new piece of land just a few miles away that desperately needs a makeover. A long time ago, this was a natural marshland.

###### Our new land for beavers

**3:11** · Then, like with so many wetlands, it was completely drained to be used for agriculture. Years later, the opposite happened. This concrete lock was installed, damming up the drainage water to create a gigantic artificial pond with millions of farmed fish where chemicals, growth hormones, and fish food polluted the water. After all of this, the land is in a pretty bad state, but that's going to change soon.

**3:37** · The beavers are already taking a curious look at this area. I am very sure they already made some plans, what they can do there.

###### The history of beavers


**3:50** · The fact that we even have beavers living here is an absolute miracle. Just 70 years ago, beavers were considered functionally extinct in the wild here in Poland. Today, the population here has grown to over 100,000 individuals, making it one of the largest beaver populations in all of Europe. But this is still a tiny number compared to the hundreds of millions. Yes, hundreds of millions of beavers that used to cover almost the entire northern hemisphere.

**4:21** · Just imagine that world for a second. It looked something like this. In fact, studies have shown that the presence of beavers in an area can triple the biodiversity there. And yet we came this close at wiping them out completely. And it was all because of this. In the 1600s, it became super fashionable across Europe to wear hats and coats made from beaver fur. Which style you chose actually said a lot about your status in society.

**4:49** · What's even weirder, beavers produce a vanilla-smelling scent from a gland right next to their butt that people turned into perfume and ice cream. I promise I'm not making this up. And sadly, for these reasons, demand for beavers absolutely skyrocketed. Once the European beaver population was depleted, the fur industry expanded to North America. And over the course of around 200 years, 99.9% of the world's beavers were hunted and killed.

**5:21** · And at the turn of the last century, only 1,200 individuals remained in Europe. The impact on nature was catastrophic. Without beavers and their dams, that complex biodiverse landscape was drained away and with it all the life that depended on it. But there is hope, because in recent decades, beavers have made a remarkable comeback, and it's largely thanks to some unconventional projects.

**5:50** · In 1948, conservationists in Idaho packed 76 beavers into wooden crates, strapped them into World War II parachutes, and literally air-dropped them into the wilderness to restore the wetlands. And the crazy plan actually worked. In Scotland, beavers were completely extinct until a few of them mysteriously appeared in the wild. Nobody's entirely sure if these beavers were illegally released or if they escaped from captivity, but today, nearly all Scottish beavers are descendants from this guerrilla population.

**6:23** · All over Europe, beavers have bounced back in one way or the other from those 1,200 individuals to over 1.5 million. And yet wetlands are still disappearing way faster than beavers can rebuild them. So every piece of land that we can give back to them is a win for nature as a whole. **6:55** · And the best part, we don't actually have to do anything because the beavers know much better than us how to do it.

Beavers love to eat the inner bark of tree branches, but instead of learning to climb up, beavers decided to bring the trees down to them. Using their self-sharpening iron-enforced teeth, they can fell a tree in a single night, strategically cutting the trunk so the tree falls into the water where it can easily be cut up and transported.

###### How beaver engineering works

**7:33** · And because beavers only eat a small portion of the tree, there's a lot of building material left to create this: dams. And they are really good at them. In Canada, they've built a dam twice the length of the Hoover Dam. Just chew on that for a moment. I mean, look at this dam right here. It's fairly new, and its construction is absolutely remarkable. Like with any good construction site, beavers follow a clear plan.

**8:01** · First, they search for a perfect location to maximise the dam's impact, choosing narrow streams in flat valleys so that even a small dam will flood a large area. Then they start digging big logs into the riverbed and anchor them with rocks to build a foundation. This then gets layered with branches, mud, and leaves to create a sturdy wall. Beavers actually monitor the sound of the water as an indicator of how well the dam stops water flow.

**8:31** · If they still hear running water, they must keep building until it's done. All of this is absolutely fascinating, but one question remains.

**8:42** · Why go through all of that work just to flood a valley?

**8:46** · Well, take a look at this mediaeval castle. It's not just protected by strong walls, but by moats of water. Beaver dams create exactly such moats to protect them from wolves and other predators. And right in the middle of it sits the beaver's lodge like a castle.

**9:04** · In German, we actually call them beaver castle, Biberburg, and there is one right over there. (peppy music) The German name really is on point as this thing is built with a multi-room layout and mud-plastered walls that are impenetrable to predators. Beavers enter through a secret tunnel that opens into a lower wet chamber for shedding water. In my anthropomorphizing mind, that's where they take off their rubber boots and hang their raincoats.

##### Description

We’re flying a Jaguar across Argentina to help protect the species.

🌱 Join us to rewild the planet: https://planetwild.com/join/m42

Every year, tens of thousands of wild animals get moved across the world for conservation.

Argentina has only 200 to 250 jaguars left, split into small, isolated groups. This shrinks their gene pool, and over generations, raises the risk of disease and can eventually wipe out a population entirely.

That’s why in our 42nd mission, we partnered with Rewilding Argentina to move Mimbi, a young female jaguar, across Argentina, to a region where introducing new genes is critical to saving the local jaguar population from inbreeding and extinction.

This translocation is part of a bigger plan: connecting isolated jaguar populations by creating a safe, continuous corridor in the South American region, so jaguars can move and mix on their own again.

People in the video:

Trishala Naidu is a South African biologist with 10 years of experience. She’s been hosting Planet Wild missions since 2024.

Guadalupe Molinaro is Rewilding Argentina's Community Program Coordinator at El Impenetrable National Park.

Pablo is Rewilding Argentina's Reintroduction Center Coordinator at Iberá Park and a wildlife conservation field technician.

Make sure to follow Rewilding Argentina: 

Website: https://rewildingargentina.org/

IG: https://www.instagram.com/rewilding_argentina/

Thanks to Wild Earth, Ami Vitale and Mike Parkei for providing additional footage.

When the mission hits unexpected complications, the team must adapt quickly to ensure the safety of this majestic endangered species. This footage provides an unfiltered look at the reality of wildlife logistics when a plan goes wrong.

##### Description

We're contributing to one of the biggest wildlife corridors in the world, a huge network of wildlife crossings, tunnels and fencing systems in North America.

🌱 Join us to rewild the planet: https://planetwild.com/join/m36

For centuries, wildlife moved freely across the Rocky Mountains. Now, roads cut through animal habitat across North America, turning simple movement into something dangerous. There are millions of wildlife collisions every year, claiming countless lives and costing billions of dollars in damages. 

We went to the Rocky Mountains and partnered with Yellowstone to Yukon (Y2Y) to contribute to a massive wildlife corridor that's reconnecting these areas and making sure wildlife can move freely again. 

But big infrastructure projects like this take extensive bureaucracy, government permits and a huge amount of public funding. And none of that happens without evidence. 

That's why, in our 36th mission, we helped Y2Y gather the data and information needed to plan future crossings and shape a landscape where humans and wildlife can coexist.

Thanks to Sean Konkolics, Government of Alberta, Miistakis and Nature Conservancy of Canada, Darryn Epp, Biodiversity Pathways, Dan Rafla and Parks Canada for providing additional pictures, and to Siobhan Williams/Wildsight for additional drone cinematography.

Virtually all the UK’s rivers have been physically altered in one way or another – straightened, dammed, dredged or restrained by barriers in some way along their course.  
 
Which is why the National Trust decided to do a radical experiment, to see if it is possible to the ecological equivalent of a complete reboot.  
 
They filled a river in west Somerset in and let it take its own course through the landscape.  
 
Our climate editor, Justin Rowlatt, has been finding out how the project worked out.

The Choco region in northwest Ecuador is hosting a groundbreaking experiment to try and help it’s rainforests recover from rampant deforestation. A multinational team is planting small “tree islands" to attract natural seed dispersers. It’s an innovative approach that we’ll take a close look at, from above and within. 

Hosted by Joe Hanson from Be Smart, Overview uses stunning 4k drone footage to reveal the natural and human made marvels shaping our planet--from a 10,000-foot view--literally.

**0:05** · (light music) Hidden along the equator lies a rainforest like no other.

**0:13** · The Choco is a kaleidoscope of life.

**0:17** · An enchanting home to an astonishing array of species many found nowhere else on Earth.

**0:24** · But like most of Earth's tropical rainforests, The Choco is under threat.

**0:29** · Widespread deforestation for agriculture, logging, and human settlements has pushed this incredible ecosystem to the brink of disappearing.

**0:37** · But, there is hope, thanks to these.

**0:41** · These are tree islands, small patches of trees replanted within larger deforested areas.

**0:47** · Scientists think this groundbreaking idea could change the world's forest recovery efforts by allowing the forest to regrow itself thanks to one surprising ingredient, animal poop.

**1:06** · (gentle music) Here in Ecuador, the Choco Rainforest covers approximately 7,000 square kilometers, nearly one and a half times the size of Grand Canyon National Park.

**1:18** · Separated from the Amazon by the towering Andes, The Choco is a world unto itself.

**1:25** · It's also one of the wettest places on Earth.

**1:29** · Some spots receiving upwards of 400 inches of rain per year.

**1:35** · It's also one of the world's most biologically diverse places.

**1:39** · A home for over 800 species of birds, 140 species of mammals, and 9,000 species of plants.

**1:50** · Here, inside a 100-meter square, you can find nearly as many tree species as in all of Europe.

**1:58** · Rainforests like The Choco are critical for preserving Earth's biodiversity.

**2:10** · These are some of the determined researchers on a mission to save this remarkable ecosystem.

**2:20** · (Leighton speaking in foreign language) - They contain more than half of all of the species in the world, even though they occupy a relatively small proportion of the Earth's land surface.

**2:29** · There's new species being discovered in tropical rainforests every year, including here in Northwestern Ecuador.

**2:35** · Every year, an area of tropical forest gets cut down that's about the size of Lake Michigan.

**2:43** · (orchestral music) - The Choco is considered one of the most threatened ecoregions in the world.

**2:48** · In Ecuador, only about 2% of the original forest cover remains.

**2:54** · As more and more of it is converted to palm oil plantations, countless species of plants and animals are at risk of extinction.

**3:09** · (Fernando speaking in foreign language) Fernando is now fighting to restore his native lands.

**3:29** · (Fernando speaking in foreign language) But saving a rainforest is not an easy task.

**3:34** · Although scientists know what a healthy tropical forest looks like, they still know very little about how to regrow them.

**3:54** · (Fernando speaking in foreign language) (light music) At this point, maybe you're thinking, why not just plant trees?

**3:58** · One new tree to replace every old one?

**4:01** · Well, the cost, for starters.

**4:03** · Additionally, many traditional replanting efforts have focused on replanting only a small number of tree species.

**4:10** · But this allows only a few fast growing species to dominate the regrown forest, and it really fails to recreate the complex diversity of species in natural rainforests, which can contain upwards of 400 tree species in an area the size of a Manhattan city block.

**4:29** · Regrowing a forest by only replanting a few species is like trying to paint a Picasso with only primary colors.

**4:39** · But here, scientists are trying something new, an idea that harnesses the power of nature itself.

**4:47** · Instead of planting rows of seedlings in a large scale plantation, the researchers are creating small, strategic patches filled with a diverse mix of native trees.

**4:58** · They hope that over time these empty spaces will be filled by the same natural processes that keep healthy rainforests lush and diverse.

**5:08** · [Leighton] The idea is that these small patches of trees will kickstart a natural regeneration process.

In a healthy rainforest, animals act as nature's gardeners. As creatures like howler monkeys and toucans feast on that fruit, their droppings disperse seeds far and wide, planting new forest with every trip to the bathroom. Up to 80% of tree species rely on birds and mammals to spread their seeds in this way.

**5:46** · When a patch of rainforest falls, it's these animal gardeners that hold the key to bringing it back to life. Eating fruits, carrying the seeds far and wide, and ultimately, planting the forest of tomorrow.

**6:00** · One of the big questions is, what are the best kinds of trees to plant?

**6:05** · How many of them do you need to plant and what kinds of spatial configurations?

**7:12** · [Joe] The project has captured the imagination of the local community.

**8:08** · Ecological restoration is not a silver bullet.

**8:12** · It's not the solution to all of our environmental problems. In order to prevent mass extinction, we have to stop destroying intact habitats. And restoration can't do that. #### Why we should be destroying more dams

**DW Planet A**, *09 18, 2026*

##### Video (11:51)

##### Description

Thousands of dams are being destroyed, bringing life back to its rivers. Migratory fish are returning to waterways, habitats are reconnecting, and entire ecosystems are being restored. While many dams remain vital for drinking water, irrigation, and flood management, Europe is 

rethinking its relationship with its rivers, one dam at a time.

We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. **0:02** · So I'm here to find out why."

**0:05** · This is the Enobieta dam.

**0:07** · Huge dams just like it can be found around the world and more are being built every year.

**0:13** · They provide clean drinking water, irrigation for farming and flood protection.

**0:17** · And they're one of the most important sources of renewable electricity on the planet.

**0:22** · But in Europe, something is changing.

**0:24** · Environmental groups want to remove thousands of dams just like this.

**0:28** · So why do they want them gone?

###### Enobieta Dam

**0:32** · "By the time you see this video, this big chunk of the dam will be gone."

**0:36** · The Enobieta Dam is named after the river it crosses.

**0:40** · This wall of concrete was built in the late 1940s to secure drinking water for San Sebastian, in northern Spain.

**0:46** · But the dam already looks different to what I expected.

**0:51** · "To me and my untrained eye, this just looks like it's a forest.

**0:55** · But what are we looking at here here?"

**0:57** · "It's indeed a forest, but all this was covered with water.

**1:02** · Here we had a reservoir which was 30-32 meters deep."

**1:07** · After San Sebastian city council decided to dismantle the dam, the reservoir was emptied in 2019.

**1:13** · Arturo Elosegi led the research into how its removal would affect the river, and the Artikutza forest that surrounds it.

**1:21** · The dam had operated for around 30 years, but it quickly became clear that there were geotechnical issues with the location.

**1:28** · Its storage capacity had to be reduced and there were also issues with iron and manganese contamination in the water.

**1:34** · And in 1976, it was abandoned altogether when a new, larger dam replaced it nearby.

**1:41** · "So they basically built this massive structure…" "In the worst place."

**1:44** · "It was obsolete almost immediately."

**1:46** · "Yeah, that's it."

**1:51** · "So we're now in the former reservoir and it seems mad that only a few years ago, this would've been just a tonne of water."

**2:01** · "Here we would be like five meters under water.

**2:05** · You can see there these big trees are the ancient ones, and the new ones, which are growing in what was the former reservoir."

**2:15** · Five years was all it took to transform the former reservoir from this… into this.

**2:20** · And then something else happened.

**2:22** · "The stream started to carve again a channel.

**2:26** · And in most of the places, it carved exactly the same channel as it had before."

**2:31** · "So the rivers returned to the exact same place… it knew where to go?"

**2:37** · "Yeah. It has memory if you want."

**2:42** · Humans have harnessed the power of water for centuries.

**2:45** · Dams have transformed modern life.

**2:47** · And hydropower remains the world's largest source of renewable energy, supplying around 14% of global electricity.

**2:56** · In Norway, hydro accounts for 95% of its electricity.

**3:00** · Its ability to reliably generate huge amounts of power means demand is still growing, even as wind and solar expand rapidly.

**3:10** · But that comes at a cost.

**3:13** · Dams interrupt the movement of fish.

**3:15** · They trap sediment, alter water temperatures and transform entire aquatic ecosystems.

**3:21** · And it's not just giant hydroelectric dams that can do this.

**3:25** · Weirs, culverts, watermills — are all barriers that can disrupt or block a river system.

**3:31** · "In Europe there are 1.2 million, at least, barriers."

**3:36** · That's Kerry Brink, who works with Dam Removal Europe, a coalition of environmental organizations working to restore free-flowing rivers across the continent.

**3:45** · "These barriers — and a large part of them are small — are really basically cutting up our river systems.

**3:52** · The water quality reduces, water is not flowing in a natural way.

**3:58** · So you really get changes in the water chemistry.

**4:01** · We have declining fish populations, our freshwater biodiversity and freshwater species are the highest impacted species globally."

**4:14** · Dam Removal Europe estimates that around 200,000 barriers are already considered obsolete.

**4:19** · Although the true number is likely much higher.

**4:23** · It's these structures, which no longer have a societal or financial benefit anymore, that they want to tear down.

**4:31** · "We are really not wanting to remove the functional barriers.

**4:37** · We are truly wanting to remove the barriers that actually have a flood risk, which actually have no purpose."

**4:47** · Across Europe, the push to remove obsolete barriers is gathering pace.

**4:51** · In 2025 alone, at least 600 came down across the continent.

**4:56** · And the European Union wants to restore at least 25,000 kilometers of free-flowing rivers by 2030.

**5:02** · But why does removing them make such a difference?

**5:08** · Part of the reason can be seen at Enobieta.

**5:11** · Because when the reservoir here was drained, an entire ecosystem returned.

**5:20** · "A small stream, in a place like this one, lives from the forest.

**5:24** · In the first year, when there was still no forest, the water was quite hot because the sunlight reached it directly.

**5:33** · But then the forest was closing and the water gets cooler."

**5:39** · As the forest returned, the food chain started to rebuild.

**5:43** · "Especially what you have is leaves.

**5:46** · And you see, this leaf is eaten by insects.

**5:48** · There are some fungi, microscopic fungi which grow on top of the leaves.

**5:55** · The insects start to eat these leaves, they grow, the fish eat the insects.

**6:02** · And so everything is fueled by these leaves.

**6:06** · The recovery has been astonishing."

**6:09** · But that recovery can only be complete when the dam itself is out of the way.

**6:21** · Instead of demolishing the whole dam, engineers and the San Sebastian City Council decided it would be enough to cut out a seven-meter section.

**6:29** · The partial removal has limited the amount of concrete taken out, minimizing heavy traffic and construction and overall disruption to the surrounding Artikutza forest.

**6:38** · It also helped protect a bat population that had colonised the dam's internal chambers.

**6:43** · And, it was significantly cheaper — costing around €1.6 million.

**6:50** · When the removal is finished and the river is reconnected, another big change will occur.

**6:56** · The river itself will start to behave naturally again, including how it moves sediment downstream.

**7:02** · Upstream there's a diverse mix of sediment, including cobbles, sand and gravel, which is distributed by the river.

**7:08** · But the dam continues to block that natural flow downstream.

**7:13** · "What you see here, these are not boulders or cobbles, these are blocks of concrete.

**7:20** · Which were thrown here when they lowered the spillway.

**7:26** · So this is totally artificial.

**7:29** · The new channel will go through there and then new sediments, natural sediments will come.

**7:33** · We can see also downstream from the dam, the river habitat was very very poor because all these sediments were retained by the reservoir."

**7:43** · When the river is allowed to pass through again, it will carry a more diverse range of sediments downstream — helping to rebuild banks, the riverbed and the habitats around it.

**7:54** · "Everything will change and we'll have again forest, the sediments will be much more natural.

**8:00** · The habitat is something that is created by the river itself when it moves the sediments.

**8:05** · And they will be created again."

**8:08** · At Enobieta, removing the dam is helping to restore this forest's unique ancient ecosystem.

**8:13** · But reconnecting rivers have other benefits too, particularly for migratory fish.

**8:21** · Which is what happened at Hiitolanjoki in Finland.

**8:24** · Three small hydropower dams had blocked movement access for the endangered landlocked Ladoga salmon.

**8:30** · Authorities decided it made sense to remove the plants and restore the rivers.

**8:35** · "What we've seen is straight after the removals, in actual fact, a week or two weeks after the removals, there was footage of these landlocked salmon spawning in the region just upstream of the barrier.

**8:50** · So it really is something that you can actually visibly see."

**8:55** · "At this point, it all sounds and looks pretty convincing.

**8:58** · Remove the barriers, the rivers reconnect, and nature returns.

**9:02** · But it's not always that simple."

**9:05** · Because while Europe is removing dams that have outlived their purpose, parts of the world are still building them.

**9:11** · Much of the Global south still needs to meet growing demands.

**9:14** · In the Democratic Republic of Congo only 1 in 5 people have access to electricity.

**9:19** · The proposed Grand Inga hydropower project could eventually generate about 42 gigawatts of power — that's about 15 times the DRC's current capacity.

**9:32** · "In many cases, there are barriers that need to be developed.

**9:39** · We do need barriers, but we just want to make sure that the barriers that are there are well functioning."

**9:46** · Meanwhile in India, the issue is more than just electricity.

**9:49** · The country of more than 1.4 billion is investing heavily in its dam network.

**9:54** · The government says they're being built to secure water supplies, support agriculture and to help control flooding.

**10:00** · But many communities, particularly in the Himalayas, have fought these new developments.

**10:05** · They claim that these dams are a threat to fragile ecosystems and disrupt the lives of local residents.

**10:10** · And as drought and flood risk increases, questions are being raised about how long some of these new dams and reservoirs can even remain effective.

**10:20** · "We need them. We have to survive.

**10:23** · So the question is to try to have as few dams as possible and to keep them working for as long as possible."

**10:33** · Some dams will remain essential for decades to come.

**10:36** · And new dams will still have to be built.

**10:38** · But Enobieta shows us that our relationship with dams needs a major rethink.

**10:43** · "Wherever you build something, you have to take into account the whole life cycle.

**10:47** · You have to take into account that someday this will be considered obsolete, it will be a danger, a hazard or whatever, and will be removed.

**10:58** · When we first started out removing this reservoir, we didn't believe we would see it.

**11:02** · I work in the environment and mostly we give bad news.

**11:06** · We look at the environment and we see problems: climate change, pollution, extinction, whatever.

**11:14** · And to see something that was barely imaginable some years ago and that's happened.

**11:22** · That's really a nice thing."

#### Wild Horses America's Most Beloved Invasive Species

**PBS Terra**, *10 22, 2020*

##### Video (8:15)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/HnOajuolHWI title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Thank you to Target for supporting PBS. You can learn more at: https://target.com/community

Share your story today: https://to.pbs.org/3izZeXh

Wild horses made their home on the islands of North Carolina centuries ago, supposedly descendants of horses brought by shipwrecked colonizers. Today, they are celebrities on these islands, creating a tourist frenzy and drawing thousands of people every summer to the northern beaches of North Carolina.

But the situation is complicated. The horse population needs to be managed because they can cause serious damage to the ecosystem. How can we respect these horses and keep them wild while protecting the islands?
